artiest/cliff-edwards.text:
Cliff Edwards was born in Hannibal, Missouri, in 1895. He left school at fourteen and sang in saloons in St. Louis. Because the pianos there were bad or missing altogether, he taught himself to play the ukulele, the cheapest instrument in the shop. A waiter gave him the nickname Ukulele Ike. His breakthrough came in 1918 in Chicago with the song Ja-Da, after which he grew into a vaudeville star and appeared in the Ziegfeld Follies.

In the 1920s Edwards was one of the most popular singers in America. He made his first records in 1919 and as early as 1922 made early examples of scat singing. He had hits with Paddlin' Madeleine Home, I Can't Give You Anything but Love and Singin' in the Rain, which he introduced in 1929. In 1924 he appeared alongside Fred and Adele Astaire in the first Broadway musical by George and Ira Gershwin, Lady Be Good. He played jazzy versions of popular songs and novelty numbers, and according to the sources he is more responsible than anyone else for the ukulele craze of those years.

After that he worked for MGM and in westerns, and on radio and television. His best-known role came in 1940: he voiced and sang Jiminy Cricket in Walt Disney's Pinocchio, and introduced When You Wish Upon a Star in it. That recording has been in the Grammy Hall of Fame since 2002. Edwards went bankrupt through squandering his money and died poor in 1971, but Disney paid for his gravestone. His voice became the sound of the Disney dream.
artiest/cliff-edwards.listen: Listen to When You Wish Upon a Star and notice Edwards's soft, almost whispering voice and the warm, old-fashioned orchestral accompaniment. Can you hear that he sings the song like a quiet lullaby?

artiest/cliff-gallup.text:
Clifton Gallup (1930 to 1988) was an American guitarist, in the 1950s the lead guitarist of Gene Vincent and His Blue Caps. His recording career was short: 35 songs with Vincent in 1956 and a solo album in the 1960s. In February 1956 the radio DJ Tex Davis heard the singer Gene Vincent at a talent night in Norfolk, Virginia. He became his manager and put together a band of local musicians. Gallup, older than Vincent and most of the others, had previously played in a local band, the Virginians.

In May 1956 the band recorded in Nashville. The producer Ken Nelson had session musicians standing by, because he feared the group would not be good enough. But as soon as Gallup played the solos of Race with the Devil, Nelson knew that was not necessary. Gallup played on Vincent's biggest hit, Be-Bop-A-Lula, and gained a reputation as one of the technically best guitarists of early rock 'n' roll. As a married man he did not want to go on tour and left the band at the end of 1956, although he returned for studio sessions for the second LP. In the 1960s he made the solo album Straight Down the Middle, in a softer instrumental style.

Gallup worked for almost thirty years in maintenance for the Chesapeake schools. At the request of his widow, newspaper reports of his death did not mention his time with Gene Vincent. Even so he inspired guitarists such as Eric Clapton, Brian Setzer and Jeff Beck, who in 1993 recorded the album Crazy Legs of songs by Vincent. Critics call him one of the greatest rockabilly guitarists ever.
artiest/cliff-gallup.listen: Listen to Race with the Devil by Gene Vincent and His Blue Caps and notice the guitar solos, which are fast and yet precise. Try to hear how the guitar throws sparks between the vocal lines.

artiest/cliff-martinez.text: Cliff Martinez was a drummer with the Red Hot Chili Peppers. After that he began writing film music, mainly for Steven Soderbergh, starting with Sex, Lies, and Videotape (1989). His music is ambient: soft, long-held sounds and small, repeated patterns. For Solaris (2002) he used, among other things, the Cristal Baschet, a glass instrument played with wet fingers, alongside steel drums and synthesizers. For Nicolas Winding Refn's Drive (2011) he wrote a cool, electronic score that fits the synth-pop songs in the film. That film made his name with a younger generation. After that he worked with Refn again on Only God Forgives (2013).
artiest/cliff-martinez.listen: Notice the soft, glittering washes of sound and the small motifs that slowly circle round without a real melody.

artiest/cliff-richard.text:
Cliff Richard was born Harry Rodger Webb in Lucknow, then still British India, in 1940. In 1948 the family moved to England, where they went to live in a simple rented house. As a teenager Harry fell under the spell of skiffle and rock 'n' roll. He became the singer of a group that was first called the Drifters. He chose his stage name in 1958: Cliff sounded like rock, and Richard was a tribute to Little Richard.

His first single was Move It from 1958, actually intended as a B-side. The song is often seen as the first real British rock 'n' roll record. With his backing group, which soon came to be called The Shadows, he dominated British pop music from the end of the 1950s to the start of the 1960s, before The Beatles. At first he was presented as a rebellious rocker in the style of Elvis Presley. After that he appeared in films such as The Young Ones and Summer Holiday, and his music became tamer and aimed at a broad audience.

Because of his Christian faith he later more often chose quiet songs and sometimes Christian pop music. He sang for the United Kingdom at the Eurovision Song Contest with Congratulations in 1968. In America he never really broke through, although he scored there with Devil Woman and We Don't Talk Anymore. In England he became one of the most successful artists ever, with hits in six decades. In 1995 he was knighted.
artiest/cliff-richard.listen: Listen to Move It from 1958. Notice the sharp electric guitar at the start and the rough vocal: here Cliff Richard still sounds like the English rocker who resembled Elvis.

artiest/clifford-brown.text: The trumpeter Clifford Brown, from Wilmington, Delaware, was encouraged as a young musician by Dizzy Gillespie and Fats Navarro. In 1954 he played on Art Blakey's A Night at Birdland and then led a quintet with the drummer Max Roach that helped shape hard bop. Brown had a warm, round tone and a technique that never sounded boastful. He wrote pieces such as Joy Spring and Daahoud. Moreover he lived without drugs or drink, which stood out in that scene. In June 1956 he was killed in a car accident at the age of 25. Benny Golson wrote I Remember Clifford in his memory. Almost all later trumpeters name him as a model.
artiest/clifford-brown.listen: Hear the round, warm tone, even in the fastest passages.

artiest/clint-mansell.text: Clint Mansell was born in Coventry in 1963. For ten years he was the singer, guitarist and songwriter of the British band Pop Will Eat Itself. After that he began a long collaboration with the director Darren Aronofsky, from Pi (1998) and Requiem for a Dream (2000) to The Fountain (2006), Black Swan (2010) and Noah (2014). Mansell has no classical training. He builds his music the way a rock band does, with drums, bass, guitar and a melody line, and works with orchestrators. For Requiem for a Dream and The Fountain the Kronos Quartet played his music. The piece Lux Aeterna was afterwards used in many film trailers. He also wrote the music for Duncan Jones's Moon (2009).
artiest/clint-mansell.listen: Notice the short, constantly repeated motif that slowly grows fuller and louder, and the mix of string quartet, electronics and rock rhythms.

artiest/clint-mansell-en-kronos-quartet.text:
Clint Mansell was born in Coventry in 1963. As a child he became hooked on the guitar through David Bowie and later the Ramones. At nineteen he joined the band that would become Pop Will Eat Itself. From 1986 to 1996 he was its singer, guitarist and one of its main writers. The group began as grebo and alt-rock, but increasingly turned to sampling and electronics, with influences from hip-hop and industrial.

After the band broke up Mansell moved to New York and later to New Orleans, where Trent Reznor helped him and introduced him to Pro Tools. In New York he met the director Darren Aronofsky. Together they made Pi, Requiem for a Dream, The Fountain, The Wrestler, Black Swan and Noah. Mansell cannot read music and builds his film music the way rock music is built: with drums, bass, guitar and melody lines, with an orchestrator to help.

The best-known piece is Lux Aeterna from Requiem for a Dream from 2000. The Kronos Quartet recorded it for the soundtrack. The piece consists of a short repeated figure that slowly swells, and became famous above all through the reworked version Requiem for a Tower, which was heard in the trailer for The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers. Since then the music has turned up in countless trailers, commercials and television programmes. Mansell later also wrote for Moon and for the films of Ben Wheatley.
artiest/clint-mansell-en-kronos-quartet.listen: Listen to Lux Aeterna and notice how little happens: the same string figure keeps returning and grows fuller and more urgent. Where do you feel the tension rise?

artiest/clyde-stubblefield.text:
Clyde Stubblefield was an American drummer, born in 1943 in Chattanooga, Tennessee. He decided to take up drumming after seeing drummers in a parade. He taught himself to play and took his sense of rhythm from the sounds of the factories and trains around him. As a teenager he was already playing in local bands. In the early 1960s he moved to Macon, Georgia, where he worked with the guitarist Eddie Kirkland and toured with Otis Redding.

In 1965 James Brown saw him play and asked him to join his band. There he shared the drums with John Jabo Starks. Neither had had lessons, and together they devised the grooves of many of Brown's big hits, such as Cold Sweat, I Got the Feelin', Say It Loud, I'm Black and I'm Proud and Mother Popcorn. His patterns are syncopated: the hits fall just off the beat, so that a simple four-four bar begins to shift and dance. In this way he helped lay the foundation of funk.

The best-known moment is his short drum solo in Funky Drummer from 1970. From the 1980s that break was sampled endlessly in hip-hop, by Public Enemy, Run-DMC, N.W.A, LL Cool J and the Beastie Boys. Stubblefield mostly received no credit for it and earned little from it. After 1971 he lived in Madison, Wisconsin, where he performed every Monday for years. He died in 2017.
artiest/clyde-stubblefield.listen: Listen to Funky Drummer by James Brown and wait for the moment when the band drops out and only the drums carry on. Notice the small accents on the snare drum and the hi-hat that fall just off the beat: that is the break that hip-hop would take over.

artiest/coldplay.text:
Coldplay is a British rock band from London. The singer and pianist Chris Martin and the guitarist Jonny Buckland met in 1996 in their first week at University College London and wrote their first songs in early 1997. The bassist Guy Berryman joined, and in January 1998 Will Champion took over the drums, actually by chance, because the drummer they were looking for did not turn up. Their friend Phil Harvey paid for the first EP and became their manager.

In 1999 the band signed to Parlophone. The debut album Parachutes from 2000 contained the breakthrough single Yellow. After that came A Rush of Blood to the Head, with Clocks and The Scientist, and X&Y, with Fix You. On Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends from 2008 the band worked with the producer Brian Eno, and the title track became a worldwide hit. Later albums such as Mylo Xyloto, Ghost Stories and Music of the Spheres took electronics, R&B, ambient and disco into the sound.

The sound of Coldplay revolves around the piano and Martin's high, soft voice, echoing guitars and big choruses that a whole hall can sing along to. In this way it is softer and more sensitive than much rock of the 1990s. In the beginning the band was compared with Radiohead and U2. Coldplay grew into one of the best-selling bands ever and is known for enormous concerts. At the same time they are controversial: too sugary for some, the biggest band of their time for others.
artiest/coldplay.listen: Listen to Yellow by Coldplay. Notice how the song begins with only guitar and Chris Martin's soft voice, and how the band then swells without ever really getting loud.

artiest/cole-porter.text:
Cole Porter was born on 9 June 1891 in Peru, Indiana, into a wealthy family. His mother had him learn music young: violin at six, piano at eight. His grandfather wanted him to become a lawyer, but Porter chose music. At Yale he wrote hundreds of songs and sang in choirs. After that he studied music in Paris for a time.

After a slow start he broke through in the 1920s, and in the 1930s he was among the most important songwriters of Broadway. Unlike many colleagues he wrote both the music and the lyrics. Musicals such as Fifty Million Frenchmen and Anything Goes yielded standards such as Night and Day, Begin the Beguine, I Get a Kick Out of You and You're the Top. After a serious riding accident in 1937 he was in pain for the rest of his life, but he kept working. In 1948 he made a great comeback with Kiss Me, Kate, based on Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew. It was his most successful musical and won the first Tony Award for best musical. He also wrote music for Hollywood, such as for High Society (1956).

Porter's songs are known for their witty, urbane lyrics full of unexpected turns and rhymes. With Irving Berlin and George Gershwin he was one of the great writers of the American song from the era of Tin Pan Alley and Broadway. Many of his songs became standards that jazz and pop singers still sing today. He died on 15 October 1964.
artiest/cole-porter.listen: Listen to You're the Top from Anything Goes (1934). Notice the lyrics: a long series of compliments that grows more and more exaggerated and funny, and how Porter makes the rhymes fall exactly on the melody.

artiest/coleman-hawkins.text: Coleman Hawkins made the tenor saxophone an important solo instrument. He played with Fletcher Henderson from 1923 to 1934 and developed a big, full tone there; the arrival of Louis Armstrong in the band in 1924 changed his sense of rhythm. From 1934 to 1939 he lived in Europe; in the Netherlands he recorded with The Ramblers in 1935 and 1937. Back in New York he recorded Body and Soul in October 1939: an improvisation that, after the first bars, almost lets go of the melody and follows the chords. Hawkins was open to new musicians; in 1944 he led one of the first bebop sessions on record, with Dizzy Gillespie. Picasso (1948) is an early solo for saxophone without accompaniment.
artiest/coleman-hawkins.listen: Listen to how in Body and Soul Hawkins plays out the chords instead of the melody.

artiest/colin-hanton.text:
Colin Hanton was born in Bootle in 1938 and grew up in Woolton, a district of Liverpool. He is an English musician, best known as the drummer of The Quarrymen, the 1950s skiffle band led by the young John Lennon. His mother died of tuberculosis in 1950, after which he went to live with his grandparents together with his brothers and sisters. He trained as a carpenter and later worked as an upholsterer. In the summer of 1956 he helped found the Quarrymen, together with Lennon, Eric Griffiths, Pete Shotton and Rod Davis. He was allowed to join mainly because he had just bought a new drum kit.

Hanton played on the group's first recordings in 1958, a cover of That'll Be the Day by The Crickets and a song written by Paul McCartney and George Harrison, In Spite of All the Danger. On 1 January 1959 he left the band after a quarrel on the way back from a failed gig at the Speke Bus Depot Social Club. By then Lennon, McCartney and Harrison were already in the group. He later heard that Pete Best was the new drummer, and lost contact. In 1997 he came together again with the surviving members of The Quarrymen for a concert marking forty years of the band. After that the group toured the United Kingdom, the United States, Germany and Japan, among other places, and he played on the albums Get Back, Together, Songs We Remember and Grey Album.

Hanton shows how The Beatles emerged from an ordinary skiffle band in Liverpool. His drumming belongs to the very first recordings of the group around Lennon.
artiest/colin-hanton.listen: Listen to That'll Be the Day in the 1958 version by The Quarrymen and notice the simple drumming and the rough recording. Try to hear how a group of youngsters plays a rock 'n' roll song.

artiest/college.text:
College is the music project of the French electronic musician David Grellier, born in 1979 and started in 2005. Grellier is also the founder of the collective Valerie and, as Mitch Silver, is part of the electroclash band Sexy Sushi. With College he wanted, in his own words, to bring together the emotions of his youth in his music. He was inspired by the American pop culture of the 1980s, by soap operas and by images of cities such as Los Angeles and Chicago, and by artists such as Daft Punk, Alan Braxe, Fred Falke and John Carpenter.

In 2008 the album Secret Diary was released, together with the EP Teenage Color. In 2011 Northern Council followed. That same year the song A Real Hero, made with the Canadian synth-pop group Electric Youth, was used in the film Drive and was a hit in France. A year later it was also heard in Taken 2. In 2013 the album Heritage came out, followed by Old Tapes in 2016 and Shanghai in 2017. In 2014 the EP Save The Day was released, with vocals by Nola Wren.

Valerie, the collective that Grellier founded in Nantes in 2007, brings together artists such as The Outrunners and Anoraak. That group is described as a romantic, retro-futuristic mix of 1980s electro, also known as synthwave. College belongs to the wave of producers who brought back the sound of the 1980s, and gained a large audience through Drive.
artiest/college.listen: Listen to A Real Hero by College and Electric Youth and notice the soft vocals and the floating synthesizers. Try to hear how the music recalls the 1980s without sounding old.

artiest/college-en-electric-youth.text:
Electric Youth is a Canadian synth-pop duo from Toronto. Bronwyn Griffin sings and writes, Austin Garrick produces, writes and plays synthesizer and drums. The two have been together since grade eight. Their breakthrough came in 2011 when their song A Real Hero, made in collaboration with College, was given a prominent place in the film Drive.

Garrick wrote the song partly in response to the pilot Chesley Sullenberger and the emergency landing of flight 1549. A Real Hero was nominated for an MTV Movie Award in 2012 and, according to Spin magazine, was among the twenty best songs of 2011. At the end of 2013 Electric Youth signed to Last Gang Records and Secretly Canadian. In 2014 the debut album Innerworld was released, with additional production by Vince Clarke of Erasure, Yazoo and Depeche Mode. Rolling Stone named the duo one of ten artists you needed to know in 2014. In 2019 Memory Emotion followed, which received a Juno Award nomination.

The music sounds like a dream of the 1980s: cool synthesizers, a steady drum machine and a clear, almost whispered singing voice. Garrick himself says that the duo does not want to imitate the past but to make something for the future. The duo's contribution to Drive helped make synthwave known to a large audience.
artiest/college-en-electric-youth.listen: Listen to A Real Hero and notice the contrast between the cool synthesizers and the soft female voice. Can you hear how the lyrics about courage sound like a quiet hymn?

artiest/collegium-vocale-gent.text:
Collegium Vocale Gent is a Belgian choir from Ghent, with instrumentalists who support the ensemble. A group of friends who were students at Ghent University founded it in 1970, on the initiative of Philippe Herreweghe. The ensemble was among the first to apply the new insights into Baroque performance practice to vocal music. The choir works with a small line-up in which the singers sing both the choral parts and the solos.

The group chose a text-centred, rhetorical approach and as a result gained a transparent, clear sound. With it, it performed in large concert halls and at festivals in Europe, Israel, the United States, Russia, South America, Japan, Hong Kong and Australia. The music of Johann Sebastian Bach soon became a speciality. That is evident from recordings such as Matthäus-Passion in 1985, Johannes-Passion in 1988, Messe in H-Moll in 1989 and Weihnachts-Oratorium in 1989, besides cantatas, motets and masses. The repertoire also reaches to Monteverdi, with Vespro della Beata Vergine in 1992, and to operas such as Orfeo ed Euridice and Zaïs.

Over the years the choir grew into an ensemble with a wide stylistic range, from Baroque to Romantic and contemporary oratorios. It works with Baroque orchestras such as the Freiburger Barockorchester and with symphony orchestras such as the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, under conductors such as Nikolaus Harnoncourt and René Jacobs. The choir also plays a role in education. Anyone who wants to hear how classical choral music can sound without heavy, Romantic tone production will find a good example in these recordings.
artiest/collegium-vocale-gent.listen: Listen to a choral section from Matthäus-Passion and notice the clear text. Can you hear how few singers are needed to keep the sound clear?

artiest/colourbox.text:
Colourbox was an English electronic group that released records on the label 4AD between 1982 and 1987. The brothers Martyn and Steve Young founded the band with Ian Robbins and the singer Debbion Currie. In 1983 Currie and Robbins left, and Lorita Grahame became the new singer. The Young brothers also played on albums by This Mortal Coil.

On 4AD, the label of dreamy bands such as Cocteau Twins and Dead Can Dance, Colourbox stood out. Their music was a colourful mix of reggae and soul, drum machine rhythms as in hip-hop, dub and industrial sounds. They covered songs by U-Roy and Augustus Pablo. The only full album, Colourbox from 1985, set hard, sample-filled instrumentals beside sad piano pieces, pop songs such as The Moon Is Blue and soul covers such as You Keep Me Hanging On. From 1983 on the group had already worked a great deal with samples.

That experience came together in 1987. Under the name M|A|R|R|S they made the song Pump Up the Volume with the group A.R. Kane, which consisted almost entirely of snippets of other records. It became an international hit, and for a pop record that way of working was new at the time. The sudden success and the lawsuits over the use of samples meant that Colourbox never recorded again. The group is thus important above all as an early pioneer of sampling culture in British dance music.
artiest/colourbox.listen: Listen to Pump Up the Volume by M|A|R|R|S. Notice how the track is built from separate snippets of other records, such as voices and rhythms, pasted over a tight dance beat.

artiest/columbia-symphony-orchestra.text:
The Columbia Symphony Orchestra was not a permanent orchestra with a concert hall of its own, but a recording orchestra of Columbia Records. The record company founded it so that it could make recordings using only its own resources. The musicians were hired by the session. They were freelancers and often members of the New York Philharmonic or the Los Angeles Philharmonic, depending on whether the recording took place in the studio on the East Coast or the West Coast.

The first recordings under this name date from as early as 1913, when Felix Weingartner made song recordings in New York with the soprano Lucille Marcel. In the 1950s the orchestra grew into the regular ensemble for Columbia's well-known conductors and soloists. In 1949 Sir Thomas Beecham, with a group of his own under this name, recorded Dance of the Hours and Carmen Suite, among other things. Later came Beethoven's Symphony no. 9 and Pastorale in 1958 and 1959, Rhapsody in Blue and An American in Paris in 1959, and piano concertos by Beethoven, Mozart and Bartók.

The list of recordings shows how broad the work was: from Baroque and classical to Gershwin and modern composers. In 1983 an album of works by Varèse also appeared, including Ionisation and Poème Électronique. The orchestra is important as an example of the studio culture of the big record labels. They put classical music on record with their own musicians and their own technology, and in this way built up a catalogue that stayed in circulation for decades.
artiest/columbia-symphony-orchestra.listen: Listen to Rhapsody in Blue from 1959 and notice the studio sound. Can you hear how clearly the different instrumental groups stand out on the record?

artiest/common.text:
Common is the stage name of Lonnie Rashid Lynn, an American rapper, actor and activist, born in 1972 in Chicago. In the beginning he was called Common Sense. At the age of twenty he signed to the independent label Relativity Records, which released his first three albums: Can I Borrow a Dollar? in 1992, Resurrection in 1994 and One Day It'll All Make Sense in 1997. In those years he built up a loyal underground following.

The breakthrough to a larger audience came through the collective Soulquarians, a group of Black musicians around neo-soul and hip-hop. On a major label came Like Water for Chocolate in 2000 and Electric Circus in 2002. In 2003 he sang and rapped on Erykah Badu's Love of My Life (An Ode to Hip-Hop), the song that gave him his highest placing in the American Hot 100 and won a Grammy. After that he signed to Kanye West's GOOD Music. There Be came out in 2005 and Finding Forever in 2007, the album with Southside. Later albums such as Nobody's Smiling in 2014 and Black America Again in 2016 deal with social themes in Black America.

His rap is thoughtful and narrative, with jazz and soul in the music beneath it. Common also worked with Karriem Riggins and Robert Glasper as August Greene, and with Pete Rock on The Auditorium Vol. 1 in 2024. Outside music he won an Oscar for Glory, the song he made with John Legend for the film Selma. He also acted in numerous films and series.
artiest/common.listen: Listen to Southside from Finding Forever and notice the way Common delivers his lyrics calmly and narratively. Can you hear how Kanye West contrasts with him?

artiest/company.text:
Company is an American band from Brooklyn, New York, founded in 2001. The members met at Bard College. There they played together in all kinds of punk groups and folk ensembles, and you can hear those two worlds in their music. Company makes songs with a basis in folk and country, but plays them with the energy of punk and psychedelic rock.

In the first years the records mostly stayed in-house. Two studio albums from the early period have never been released, nor has a live album. In 2004 the third album, Hills, was released independently. The fourth, Parallel Time, was released in October 2005 by Brah Records, the label of the band Oneida. The second album on that label, Old Baby, came out in February 2008 and was produced by Kid Millions of Oneida. In those years Company often shared a bill with label-mates such as Oakley Hall, Oneida, Home and Dirty Faces.

In 2014 the television series The Vampire Diaries used the song Poisonous Spider from the album Over the Mountain. That same year the band released its first LP on its own label Papasan Recordings. Company consists of three songwriters and a drummer, who swap instruments among themselves: guitar, bass, keyboards, violin and harmonica all come by. It is a small band from the American independent scene that went its own way outside the big labels.
artiest/company.listen: Listen to a track from Parallel Time and notice the combination of folk-like singing with a rough, punk-like guitar. Which of the two wins?

artiest/comtessa-de-dia.text:
The Comtessa de Dia, the countess of Die, was a trobairitz: a female troubadour from the south of France. She was active around 1175 or around 1212; we do not know more precisely than that. Her name too is uncertain. She may have been called Beatritz or Isoarda. In the sources from her time she is called only the countess of Die, a small town north-east of Montélimar. She was presumably the daughter of Count Isoard II of Die. According to her vida, the short biography that has been preserved with the songs, she was married to William of Poitiers, but loved Raimbaut of Orange and sang about him.

Five pieces of her work have survived: four cansos and a tenson. She sang in Occitan, the language of the troubadours. Her subjects are optimism, praise of herself and her love, but also betrayal. In A chantar m'er de so qu'ieu non volria she plays an abandoned lover who nevertheless keeps defending and praising herself.

That song is the reason her name counts in music history. It is the only canso by a trobairitz whose melody has also survived. It appears in Le Manuscript du roi, a song collection copied around 1270 for Charles of Anjou, the brother of Louis IX. It is therefore one of the few places where we can really hear how a medieval woman sang her own love songs.
artiest/comtessa-de-dia.listen: Listen to A chantar m'er de so qu'ieu non volria and notice the melody, which comes from the Manuscript du roi. Can you hear how the melody follows the text?

artiest/concertgebouworkest.text:
The Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra is a Dutch symphony orchestra from Amsterdam. It was founded in 1888, a few months after the Concertgebouw opened, and gave its first concert on 3 November of that year under the first chief conductor, Willem Kes. In 1988, in honour of its centenary, the orchestra received the prefix Royal. It is regarded as one of the best orchestras in the world.

It is remarkable that in more than a hundred years the orchestra had only seven chief conductors. Willem Mengelberg stayed from 1895 to 1945 and brought the orchestra to an international level, with a preference for Gustav Mahler and Richard Strauss. After him came, among others, Eduard van Beinum, Bernard Haitink, Riccardo Chailly and Mariss Jansons. The orchestra had a special bond with Mahler and held a Mahler festival in 1920. Almost a thousand recordings have been made of it. The list begins with Beethoven, with the Eroica and the Symphony no. 7 in 1950, and runs via Mahler's Le Chant de la Terre to Brahms and Bruckner.

For pop lovers the orchestra is interesting above all as a yardstick. Anyone who wants to hear how a great symphony orchestra sounds when playing in a hall with famous acoustics will find the reference here. The orchestra also plays in operas of the Dutch National Opera and releases its own recordings on the label RCO Live. It is thus an example of an institution that keeps classical music of all centuries alive.
artiest/concertgebouworkest.listen: Listen to a recording of Beethoven's Symphony no. 3 Eroica by the orchestra and notice how the strings and winds take turns. Which group takes over the melody?

artiest/concerto-italiano.text:
Concerto Italiano is an Italian early music ensemble, known for its performances of Monteverdi and Vivaldi. The harpsichordist Rinaldo Alessandrini founded the group. The ensemble plays according to the principles of historically informed performance practice: with the instruments and playing styles of the time in which the music originated. In 1984 it made its debut in Rome with La Calisto by Francesco Cavalli.

In the 1990s the group recorded the madrigals of Monteverdi. The Quarto Libro dei Madrigali appeared in 1993, Il sesto libro de madrigali in 1992. Those recordings won many prizes, including three Gramophone Awards. Palestrina, Cavalli and other early composers also appear in the list, with titles such as Arie Musicali and Cain, overo il primo omicidio. The ensemble recorded for Opus 111, which now belongs to the French label Naïve.

Later the group devoted itself to Vivaldi. Together with the university library of Turin, Concerto Italiano recorded all of Vivaldi's operas and concertos, many pieces of which had not been played for more than three hundred years. According to Gramophone, Le Quattro Stagioni was one of the best performances of that work. For the Vespri Solenni per la Festa dell'Assunzione di Maria Vergine the group received a Gramophone Award in 2004. In this way Concerto Italiano showed that Baroque music from Italy can sound passionate and dramatic.
artiest/concerto-italiano.listen: Listen to a madrigal by Monteverdi, for example from the Quarto Libro dei Madrigali. Notice how the singers bring the text to life with small shifts in tempo and sound.

artiest/concerto-italiano-en-rinaldo-ale.text:
Concerto Italiano is an Italian early music ensemble known for its performances of Monteverdi and Vivaldi. The harpsichordist Rinaldo Alessandrini founded it. The ensemble plays according to historical performance practice, that is, with the instruments and playing styles of the time of the music itself. It made its debut in Rome in 1984 with La Calisto by Francesco Cavalli.

After that Concerto Italiano recorded the madrigals of Monteverdi. Those recordings won many prizes, including three Gramophone Awards, and also the German record critics' prize, the Académie Charles Cros and the Vivaldi prize of the Fondazione Cini. The ensemble was under contract to Opus 111, which later belonged to the French label Naïve. Together with the university library of Turin it began recording all of Vivaldi's operas and concertos, part of which had not been performed for more than three hundred years. The highlights include the opera L'Olimpiade, La Senna Festeggiante and a version of Le Quattro Stagioni that Gramophone called one of the best.

In the course, the ensemble represents the madrigal around 1600, the form in which poets and composers wrote out feelings down to the smallest details. Alessandrini and his singers let you hear how strongly that music moves with the words: every turn in the text is given a sound of its own. That makes their recordings suitable for hearing why Italian madrigalists became so famous.
artiest/concerto-italiano-en-rinaldo-ale.listen: Listen to Moro, lasso, al mio duolo and notice the sudden switches between slow and fast and between grating and calm harmony. How does the music follow the words about pain and dying?

artiest/concerto-palatino.text:
The name Concerto Palatino has had two lives. The original Concerto Palatino was a wind ensemble and an important civic institution in Bologna, attached to the basilica of San Petronio. The group gave concerts in the city every morning and evening. It began in the thirteenth century as a small group of eight trumpeters. At the end of the fifteenth century trombones were added. From 1537 to 1779 the line-up was fixed: eight trumpets, four pifari, later cornetts, four trombones, two violins and drums. The members also taught at the Liceo.

In 1986 the cornettist Bruce Dickey and the trombonist Charles Toet revived the name for a new ensemble. It was one of the first groups to play the repertoire of the original alta capella according to the principles of historically informed performance practice, that is, on instruments and with playing styles of the period itself.

The recordings show a broad repertoire. They include titles such as Musica Religiosa in 1992, Early Music of the Netherlands 1400-1600 in 1993, Vespro della beata Vergine in 1995, Selva morale e spirituale in 2001 and Altbachisches Archiv in 2003. In this way the group lets you hear how cornetts and trombones sounded in churches and on squares, before the modern symphony orchestra existed.
artiest/concerto-palatino.listen: Listen to Vespro della beata Vergine and notice the sound of the cornetts and trombones. Can you hear how warm and singing those wind instruments sound, compared with a modern trumpet?

artiest/cong-su.text:
Cong Su is a composer who was born in Tianjin, China, in 1957 and later went to live in Germany. From 1978 to 1982 he studied at the Central Conservatory of Music in Beijing and then in Germany, at the music academy in Munich. There he learned music theory, music analysis, film music and ballet music, and later taught himself. Since 1991 he has been professor of film and media composition at the film academy in the Stuttgart region. He divides his time between Beijing, Lake Constance and Lucca in Italy.

His best-known work is the music for The Last Emperor, Bernardo Bertolucci's 1987 film. Cong Su wrote that music together with Ryuichi Sakamoto and David Byrne. Together they won the Oscar for best original score. The soundtrack album The Last Emperor: Original Motion Picture Soundtrack received a Grammy in 1989 for best score for visual media.

After that he went on mainly writing film music, chiefly for Asian films. Examples are Green Tea in 2002 and Jasmine Women in 2004. In 2011 Empire of Silver appeared as a soundtrack album. His name thus stands for the musical bridge between East and West in the film world: a Chinese composer who trains and works in Europe.
artiest/cong-su.listen: Listen to an excerpt from the soundtrack of The Last Emperor and notice how the music carries the scene. What mood does the sound evoke in you, and which instruments do you hear?

artiest/conlon-nancarrow.text:
Conlon Nancarrow was born in Texarkana, Arkansas, in 1912 and died in Mexico City in 1997. In his youth he played trumpet in a jazz band, then studied music in Cincinnati and Boston. He joined the American Communist Party and fought in the Spanish Civil War with the International Brigades. In 1940 he moved to Mexico, to escape the harassment in the United States. In 1956 he became a Mexican citizen. He lived there for a long time in seclusion.

In Mexico he made the work for which he became known: Studies for Player Piano. His compositions were so difficult that two human hands could hardly play them. He therefore bought a machine for punching rolls for a mechanical piano. In doing so he followed a suggestion from Henry Cowell's book New Musical Resources. The piano could play complicated rhythms at a speed beyond the reach of humans. Nancarrow was one of the first composers to use self-playing instruments in this way.

Not until the 1980s did he become widely known. In 1977 the first series of recordings of his piano rolls appeared on 1750 Arch Records, and in 1982 he received a MacArthur Award. György Ligeti called his music the greatest discovery since Webern and Ives. Nancarrow is regarded as a forerunner of later electronic music with extremely fast notes, such as Black MIDI. His entire studio, with the piano rolls, is now held by the Paul Sacher Foundation in Basel.
artiest/conlon-nancarrow.listen: Listen to one of the Studies for Player Piano and notice the rhythms running through one another. Can a human play this, do you think?

artiest/connie-kay.text:
Connie Kay, born Conrad Henry Kirnon, was born in 1927 and died in New York in 1994. He was an American drummer in jazz and rhythm and blues, and a member of the Modern Jazz Quartet. Kay taught himself to drum and played in Los Angeles in the mid-1940s. His playing can be heard on The Hunt, the recording of a famous jam session in 1947 in which the tenor players Dexter Gordon and Wardell Gray played against each other. From 1949 to 1955 he played in Lester Young's quintet, and he worked with Stan Getz, Coleman Hawkins, Charlie Parker and Miles Davis.

In the early 1950s he did sessions for Atlantic Records. You can hear him on hits such as Shake, Rattle and Roll by Big Joe Turner and (Mama) He Treats Your Daughter Mean by Ruth Brown. In 1955 he took Kenny Clarke's place in the Modern Jazz Quartet. He stayed until the group broke up in 1974, and also played at reunions. With the alto saxophonist Paul Desmond, a representative of Cool Jazz, he had a lasting partnership in the first half of the 1960s.

He also left traces in pop music. He played drums on several of Van Morrison's albums: Astral Weeks, a track on Saint Dominic's Preview and four tracks on Tupelo Honey. Kay was known for the percussion he used alongside his drum kit, such as timpani, small cymbals, triangle, bell tree and darbukas. As a leader he never recorded an album of his own.
artiest/connie-kay.listen: Listen to Astral Weeks by Van Morrison and notice Connie Kay's drumming. Can you hear how the drums accompany the vocals instead of laying down a solid beat?

artiest/cootie-williams.text:
Cootie Williams was born in Mobile, Alabama, in 1911 and died in New York in 1985. He was an American trumpeter in jazz, jump blues and rhythm and blues. He began as a professional musician at the age of fourteen in the Young Family band, in which the saxophonist Lester Young also played. In 1928 he made his first records in New York with the pianist James P. Johnson. After that he played briefly with Chick Webb and Fletcher Henderson.

He made his name as a member of Duke Ellington's orchestra, which played at the Cotton Club. He was in that band from 1929 to 1940. He was known for his jungle style on the trumpet, in the line of Bubber Miley and Tricky Sam Nanton, and for his use of the plunger mute, a small mute that makes the sound growl and talk. Ellington wrote Concerto for Cootie for him, which, with lyrics, became Do Nothing till You Hear from Me. He was also the soloist in pieces such as Echoes of Harlem and Harlem Air Shaft.

In 1940 he moved to Benny Goodman's orchestra, which caused a great stir. In 1941 he started his own orchestra, in which Charlie Parker, Eddie Lockjaw Davis and Bud Powell, among others, played. In the 1950s he played more rhythm and blues. At the end of the 1950s came albums such as The Big Challenge and Porgy and Bess Revisited. In 1962 he returned to Ellington and stayed until 1974. In this way he links the swing era with the later rhythm and blues.
artiest/cootie-williams.listen: Listen to Do Nothing till You Hear from Me and notice the trumpet solo, in particular the sound that resembles a singing voice. Can you hear the muted, growling tone?

artiest/corry-brokken.text:
Corry Brokken was born in Breda in 1932 and died in 2016. She was a singer, television presenter and lawyer. In 1956 she won the Nationaal Songfestival, the Dutch national selection, with Voorgoed voorbij, with which she represented the Netherlands in the first Eurovision Song Contest. A year later she won the national song contest again and went once more to the international stage. Her song Net als toen, written by Willy van Hemert and composed by Guus Jansen, received the most points from the international juries. It was the first Dutch victory in the contest.

In 1958 she took part again, this time with Heel de wereld. That song finished in last place in the final in Hilversum, with one point. She is thus the only singer ever to have come both first and last in this song contest. In the 1950s and 1960s she sang in the Sleeswijk Revue with Snip and Snap and scored hits, including translated chansons by Charles Aznavour. Albums from her career include Corry's Bed-Time Story in 1960 and Wereldsuccessen in 1968.

In 1973 she stopped singing to study law. She became a lawyer and later a judge in Den Bosch. In 1976 she presented the Eurovision Song Contest in The Hague. In the 1990s she returned to the stage and recorded a new album, Nooit gedacht. Corry Brokken is a milestone in Dutch pop history because she was the first Dutch person to win the Eurovision Song Contest.
artiest/corry-brokken.listen: Listen to Net als toen and notice the singing style: a clear voice with a carefully shaped song. Can you hear how that sound fits the 1950s?

artiest/count-basie.text: William 'Count' Basie came from Red Bank, New Jersey, learned stride piano in Harlem, where Fats Waller also taught him to play the organ, and ended up stranded in Kansas City in the 1920s. He played with Bennie Moten and, after Moten's death in 1935, started a band of his own at the Reno Club. The producer John Hammond heard him on the radio and brought the band to New York. Basie played strikingly few notes: short, well-placed chords. His rhythm section, with the guitarist Freddie Green, the bassist Walter Page and the drummer Jo Jones, became famous for its light, even swing. With the tenor saxophonist Lester Young and the singer Jimmy Rushing, the band had great soloists. In the 1950s Basie started a second orchestra with tighter arrangements.
artiest/count-basie.listen: Notice the piano: a few notes, exactly at the right moment.

artiest/count-basie-and-his-orchestra.text:
Count Basie arrived in Kansas City in 1927, played with Walter Page and Bennie Moten and, after Moten's death in 1935, started his own group. That nine-piece band, with Lester Young on tenor sax, Jo Jones on drums and Walter Page on bass, among others, brought the Kansas City jam session to the clubs: long improvised solos over riffs from the band. In 1936 the producer John Hammond heard the group on the radio. He had Basie expand it into a big band and brought him to New York.

In January 1937 the orchestra made its first records for Decca. One O'Clock Jump from 1937 and Jumpin' at the Woodside from 1938 followed, which made the orchestra famous nationally and internationally. They were so-called head arrangements: not written out, but built from riffs that the musicians knew by heart. With the guitarist Freddie Green one of the best-known rhythm sections in big band history was complete, and the singer Jimmy Rushing brought the blues.

After a short break in the early 1950s Basie built a new orchestra, with arrangers such as Neal Hefti, Quincy Jones and Sammy Nestico. Albums such as The Atomic Mr. Basie from 1958 and April in Paris showed a tighter and fuller ensemble, in which the arrangements became more important than the soloists. The orchestra worked with Frank Sinatra, Ella Fitzgerald and Joe Williams, and has continued to exist since Basie's death in 1984.
artiest/count-basie-and-his-orchestra.listen: Listen to One O'Clock Jump and notice how the band answers the soloists with short riffs. Can you hear how the rhythm section keeps swinging along calmly while the soloists are given room?

artiest/count-lasher.text:
Count Lasher was the stage name of Terence Parkins, a Jamaican singer and songwriter who was born around 1921 and died in 1977. He came from the mountainous district of Saint Thomas. His music was mainly mento, first in a rural and later in an urban style. Mento is the folk music of Jamaica that preceded the sound of ska and reggae. In later years he also recorded a few ska and reggae singles. His age and the spelling of his real name are still disputed.

Lasher began his career shortly after leaving school. He taught himself to play piano and guitar and travelled to Kingston, where he entertained tourists on boats in the harbour. He performed in hotels, at beach parties, at charity events and sometimes in cinemas before the film began. His debut was produced by Stanley Motta. He played with changing backing bands, such as Count Lasher's Seven, the Royal Calypsonians and Calypso Quartet. Many Jamaican artists then used names with calypso in them, because tourists knew that term better.

In his songs Lasher is a storyteller and a social commentator. He uses a great deal of colourful dialect and subjects that the island's inhabitants recognised at once, as in Mango Time. He made more than fifty songs, but never an album. The musicologist Michael Garnice calls him perhaps the most neglected artist in Jamaican recording history.
artiest/count-lasher.listen: Listen to Mango Time and notice the list of mango varieties in the chorus. Can you hear how the song tells a story from everyday life in Jamaica?

artiest/courtney-pine.text:
Courtney Pine was born in London in 1964, the son of Jamaican immigrants. He studied classical clarinet at school and from the age of fourteen taught himself to play saxophone. His career began in reggae: in 1981 he toured with the duo Clint Eastwood & General Saint. Later he grew into one of the best-known British jazz musicians. He plays mainly saxophone, but also flute, clarinet, bass clarinet and keyboards. On Europa from 2011 he plays almost only bass clarinet.

In 1985 he founded the Jazz Warriors, a Black British big band that grew out of a community band that played in the foyer of the Royal Festival Hall in the summer of International Youth Year. In 1987 the group recorded Out of Many, One People for Antilles, a part of Island Records. In 1986 his debut album Journey to the Urge Within reached the British top 40. After that came, among others, Destiny's Song & The Image of Pursuance in 1988, Modern Day Jazz Stories in 1995, Underground in 1997 and Transition in Tradition, a tribute to Sidney Bechet, in 2009.

In the 2000s he mixed jazz with drum and bass and UK garage. In 1989 he also played with the Pet Shop Boys, in the closing section of their single Nothing Has Been Proved. On BBC Radio 2 he presented the programme Jazz Crusade. His influence therefore lies not only in his playing, but also in the space he made for Black British jazz.
artiest/courtney-pine.listen: Listen to a track from Journey to the Urge Within and notice the saxophone. Can you hear how it sings over the rhythm?

artiest/coxsone-dodd.text:
Clement Seymour Dodd, nicknamed Coxsone, was born in Kingston in 1932 and died in 2004. He was a Jamaican producer with great influence on the development of ska and reggae. He got his nickname at school, because he was so good at cricket that friends compared him with the cricketer Alec Coxon. As a boy Dodd played records for the customers in his parents' shop. During a stay in the southern United States he got to know the rhythm and blues that was popular there.

In 1954, back in Jamaica, he set up the Downbeat Sound System, with an amplifier, a turntable and American records from New Orleans and Miami. He opened five sound systems, which played every night, and gave people such as Lee Perry, U-Roy and Prince Buster a job. When rhythm and blues went out of fashion in America, he had to have Jamaican music recorded himself. In 1959 he founded the label Worldisc, and in 1963 he opened Studio One on Brentford Road in Kingston, the first studio in Jamaica owned by a Black owner.

In the early 1960s he produced ska by Toots and the Maytals, the Gaylads and the Skatalites. At his Sunday evening auditions Bob Marley dropped by with the Wailers. In the late 1960s and in the 1970s the Studio One sound was a byword for ska, rocksteady and reggae, with artists such as Burning Spear, Delroy Wilson, Horace Andy and Sugar Minott. His song You're Wondering Now was later covered by the Specials and Amy Winehouse, among others.
artiest/coxsone-dodd.listen: Listen to You're Wondering Now in a version by the Skatalites or the Specials and notice the rhythmic ticks on the second and fourth beats. Can you hear how that ska rhythm carries the song?

artiest/craig-armstrong.text: Craig Armstrong was born in 1959 in Shettleston, a district of Glasgow. From 1977 to 1981 he studied composition, violin and piano at the Royal Academy of Music in London. In 1994 he contributed to Massive Attack's album Protection. His first solo albums then appeared on their label Melankolic. For the director Baz Luhrmann he wrote Romeo + Juliet (1996), Moulin Rouge! (2001) and The Great Gatsby (2013), films in which pop songs and orchestral music run together. For Moulin Rouge! he won a Golden Globe and a BAFTA. Other scores are Love Actually (2003), Ray (2004), for which he received a Grammy, and Far from the Madding Crowd (2015). In 2010 he was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire.
artiest/craig-armstrong.listen: Listen to how a simple piano theme is built up with strings, with the calm repetition and tone colour of pop production instead of classical development.

artiest/craig-david.text:
Craig David was born in Southampton in 1981. His father, who came from Grenada, played bass in a reggae band. As a teenager Craig went along to local dance clubs, where DJs gave him the microphone, and soon he was writing songs of his own and working as an MC and DJ in youth centres. His first visible work was vocals on a B-side and on songs by the garage duo Artful Dodger, such as Something and What Ya Gonna Do.

In 1999 his breakthrough came with Re-Rewind (The Crowd Say Bo Selecta) by Artful Dodger, a song that reached number two in the British charts. That allowed him to continue as a solo artist at Wildstar Records. His first single Fill Me In became a number one in England, and the debut album Born to Do It from 2000 produced more hits, such as Walking Away and 7 Days. The album sold more than eight million copies worldwide. The follow-up Slicker Than Your Average appeared in 2002, and later came, among others, The Story Goes..., Trust Me, Following My Intuition and 22. He collaborated with Sting and Kano, among others.

Craig David's music combines the rhythms of British garage with soft R&B and a smooth singing voice. He wrote his debut album almost entirely with Mark Hill of Artful Dodger. In this way he grew in a short time from guest singer on a dance track into a star of his own in British R&B around the turn of the century.
artiest/craig-david.listen: Listen to Re-Rewind and notice the jumps in the rhythm and Craig David's quick, almost rapped vocals. Can you hear how the crowd is drawn in by the shouting of Rewind?

artiest/cream.text:
Cream was a British rock group that came into being in London in 1966 from three celebrated musicians: the bassist Jack Bruce, the guitarist Eric Clapton and the drummer Ginger Baker. Clapton had made a name with the Yardbirds and John Mayall & the Bluesbreakers; Baker and Bruce came from Graham Bond's band. Because they were already considered the cream of the British blues and jazz scene, they called themselves Cream. They are often regarded as the first supergroup in rock history.

In three years the group released four albums: Fresh Cream in 1966, Disraeli Gears in 1967, Wheels of Fire in 1968 and Goodbye in 1969. From Disraeli Gears the producer Felix Pappalardi worked with them. That album contained Sunshine of Your Love, their biggest American hit. Wheels of Fire was the first double album to go platinum. Bruce wrote most of the songs and sang; Clapton and Baker also contributed. There was always tension between Bruce and Baker, and in 1968 they decided to stop. In November of that year they gave two farewell concerts at the Royal Albert Hall.

The music moved between blues rock, psychedelia and hard rock. Live, the band stretched songs into long improvisations, and on Toad Baker played one of the first drum solos in rock. The trio showed what three virtuoso instrumentalists could do in a line-up without a second guitarist. In 1993 Cream was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/cream.listen: Listen to White Room and notice how the guitar, the bass and the drums each play a role of their own. Where do you hear Bruce's singing, and where does the guitar take over?

artiest/creedence-clearwater-revival.text:
Creedence Clearwater Revival, CCR for short, was an American rock band from El Cerrito, California. The band members were the singer, lead guitarist and writer John Fogerty, his brother Tom Fogerty on rhythm guitar, the bassist Stu Cook and the drummer Doug Clifford. They had been playing together since 1959, first as the Blue Velvets and later as the Golliwogs. In 1968 they adopted the name Creedence Clearwater Revival, after Saul Zaentz had bought the label Fantasy.

The breakthrough came with the cover of Susie Q in 1968. In 1969 came Bayou Country with Proud Mary, Green River and Willy and the Poor Boys, with Down on the Corner and Fortunate Son. Bad Moon Rising was number one in England for three weeks. Between 1969 and 1971 the group had fourteen consecutive singles in the American top ten and five albums in the top ten. In 1969 the band played at Woodstock. Cosmo's Factory came in 1970, Pendulum in 1970 and Mardi Gras in 1972, the year in which the group split up in acrimony.

The music is simple and direct: roots rock, inspired by Little Richard, Hank Williams, Elvis Presley and Chuck Berry. In contrast to the psychedelic scene of San Francisco, CCR deliberately chose basic rock and roll. Proud Mary became the group's most covered song, among others by Ike and Tina Turner in 1971. The music remains a fixture on American classic rock stations.
artiest/creedence-clearwater-revival.listen: Listen to Bad Moon Rising and notice the contrast between the cheerful melody and the ominous lyrics. Can you hear how simply guitar, bass and drums stay together?

artiest/crisol.text:
Crisol is the name of a group that the trumpeter Roy Hargrove put together around 1997. The Spanish word means melting pot, and that suits the music: jazz with Afro-Cuban rhythms. Hargrove brought in top jazz players and Cuban percussionists. The line-up on the album Grande-Terre, recorded in April 1998, consisted of Hargrove himself, the saxophonists Sherman Irby and Jacques Schwarz-Bart, the trombonist Frank Lacy, the guitarist Ed Cherry, the pianists Larry Willis and Gabriel Hernández, the bassist Gerald Cannon, the drummers Willie Jones and Julio Barreto and the percussionists Changuito and Miguel Angá Díaz.

An earlier recording by the group, Habana, was made on 5 and 6 January 1997. Grande-Terre was left on the shelf for a long time and was not released until 18 October 2024, on Verve, without edits or overdubs. The song Kamala's Dance is named after Hargrove's daughter, born in 1997. In Priorities Julio Barreto sings an introductory greeting in the Abakuá language, which belongs to an initiation.

Reviewers praised the intricate arrangements, the powerful horn sound and Hargrove's driving playing. According to one critic, the Afro-Cuban rhythms sounded more authentic than on old Blue Note records. Crisol thus reveals a side of Hargrove that is little known outside the jazz world.
artiest/crisol.listen: Listen to Priorities on Grande-Terre and notice the sung opening greeting by Julio Barreto. Can you hear how the percussion then sets the song in motion?
